segments.en: Deep in the rainforest, a river suddenly drops off the edge of a cliff. This is Kaieteur Falls, a single, thundering curtain of water plunging into a gorge, with mist rising and swifts darting in and out behind it.

Guyana sits on the northern shoulder of South America. Its name is often said to mean land of many waters, and rivers are everywhere: the Essequibo, the Demerara and the Berbice all flow north to the Atlantic.

It is the only country in South America where English is the official language, and it feels closely tied to the Caribbean. Everyday talk is in Guyanese Creole, lively and full of its own expressions.
Most people live along the narrow coastal strip, much of which lies below sea level at high tide. Long sea walls and canals, first dug centuries ago, keep the ocean out and the fields dry.

Georgetown, the capital, has wide avenues lined with trees and white wooden buildings. St. George's Cathedral is one of the tallest wooden churches in the world, and Stabroek Market, with its iron clock tower, bustles all day.

Guyana's people have roots in many places: Indigenous nations who have always lived here, and families who came from Africa, India, China and Portugal. That mix shapes everything, from festivals to food.

So the calendar is full. Diwali lights up homes with little clay lamps, Phagwah fills the streets with coloured powder, Christmas and Eid are celebrated by neighbours of every faith, and in February, Mashramani brings a parade of costumes and steel bands.

The dish for Christmas morning is pepperpot, a dark, slow-cooked meat stew flavoured with cassareep, a sauce made from cassava by Indigenous cooks. Curry and roti, cook-up rice and metemgee are everyday favourites.

Inland, the forest stretches for hundreds of kilometres, one of the most untouched rainforests on the planet. Giant river otters, jaguars and harpy eagles live here, and the Rupununi savanna opens into rolling grassland.

In the Rupununi, Indigenous communities welcome visitors to their villages, share their knowledge of the forest, and help protect the black caiman and the giant water lilies that float on quiet lakes.
Cricket is a national love, and Guyanese players have starred for the West Indies team. On a Sunday, you'll find games on every open field, with plenty of cheering from the shade.
Listen to the river one more time as it rolls toward the sea. When you're ready, cross the Corentyne River into Suriname, Guyana's neighbour to the east.
